bib.title: Pseudoreplication: Choose Your Data Wisely (Chapter 3, Statistics Done Wrong)

question: How does treating dependent measurements as independent samples inflate apparent sample size and invalidate hypothesis tests, and how can it be avoided or corrected?

results.claim: Worked example: 10 patients measured 100 times each gives 1,000 data points per group but only 10 unique patients, so the apparent sample size and power are illusory.
results.setup: Blood pressure drug comparison; design A 2,000 patients randomized (1,000 per group), design B 10 patients with 100 measurements each
results.quote: I still have 1,000 data points per group but only 10 unique patients.

results.claim: Worked example: two cycles of 28 and roughly 30 days drift apart by two days, then four, so unaligned cycles pass in and out of alignment by chance; the synchronization test's null assumed random increases and decreases.
results.setup: Critique of McClintock early-1970s Nature study of menstrual synchronization
results.quote: Their cycles will diverge consistently over the course of the study, starting two days apart, then four days, and so on

results.claim: Statistical corrections for dependence usually give wider confidence intervals and larger p values than the naive analysis.
results.setup: Any analysis adjusted for dependent measurements
results.quote: (This means they usually give wider confidence intervals and larger p values than the naive analysis.)

results.claim: Maximum gap between period starts of two women with a 28-day cycle is 14 days, so the average is seven days and periods often overlap by chance.
results.setup: Average cycle 28 days, periods lasting five to seven days
results.quote: That’s the maximum, so the average will be seven days

results.claim: Later work with corrected statistics found no evidence of estrous or menstrual synchronization, though this is controversial.
results.source: endnote 13, not printed in this PDF
results.setup: Human, rodent and chimpanzee synchronization studies
results.quote: Subsequent research using corrected statistical methods has failed

limits: No data or experiments of its own; all examples are illustrative or cited from endnotes whose list is not in this PDF.
Author concedes the estrous/menstrual synchronization finding is controversial.
Statistical fixes do not eliminate dependence, only quantify it; poor design cannot be rescued.
practices: Ensure the analysis answers the research question; extra dependent measurements only raise certainty about the specific sample, not the population (Tips, p.38).
Use hierarchical models or clustered standard errors when measurements are strongly dependent (Tips, p.38).
Design to eliminate hidden correlation, and record confounders so they can be adjusted for (Tips, p.38).
Average dependent points per subject, using a weighted analysis if subjects were measured unequally often (p.34).
Analyze each dependent time point separately, but beware multiple comparisons (p.34).
Adjust p values and CIs via clustered standard errors, repeated measures tests or hierarchical models (p.34).
Randomly assign treatments to blocks within each field rather than one treatment per field (p.33).
Split each biological group evenly across microarray batches, record batch processing, storage and reagents, and use PCA to check for batch effects (p.35).
Randomize assignment to groups to prevent systematic bias and hidden confounding (p.32).

terms.definition: Treating non-independent measurements (same subject, culture, aquarium, batch, or one recording) as independent samples, so the data answer the wrong question.
Test subjects are assigned to experimental or control groups randomly, rather than for any systematic reason.
Repeated measurements of the same subject over time are dependent on one another.
Systematic variation from the processing batch (machine, lab, reagents, day) rather than the biology.
Subjects housed together may influence one another, making them not independent.
